quote: That it was gonna cost me a $127 a month. And I was like, that's no savings.
stewart_read: This is a textbook cost objection where the flip ("what's not saving you money is your current $138 bill") was directly available given the customer had just anchored their own bill number. The rep never deploys it.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep might be strategically diagnosing the full objection before pivoting, but no pivot ever follows in the rest of the call, so the reactive read holds.
coaching_implication: Drill the rep on immediately flipping a stated bill number into the reason to act, per coaching_philosophy.objection_inversion, the moment the customer states their own bill.

quote: my average utility bill is a $138.
stewart_read: Customer volunteers a clean bill anchor unprompted. This is exactly the number the bill-anchoring flip pattern (ask + acknowledge + flip) needs, but the rep only acknowledges the number for comparison math, never emotionally flips it.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to treat any customer-volunteered bill figure as the anchor point for reframing, not just an input for arithmetic.

quote: Okay. I see what you're saying. Yeah. Well, did you know that I don't know if you are aware, but solar actually has an end date.
stewart_read: The rep moves into explaining solar payoff mechanics and product structure — closer-tier financial education — rather than using the universal escape hatch to redirect to a specialist or to a curiosity-creation move.
alternative_hypothesis: This could be viewed as necessary rebuttal content since the schema does include an educational rebuttal path, but the schema's curiosity_over_features principle argues against unprompted feature/mechanism explanation at setter stage.
coaching_implication: Show the rep the escape hatch language ("that's exactly what the specialist walks through") as an alternative to explaining payoff timelines himself.

quote: Hey. The lie was that the the Virginia Power was putting them up there for free, which I know is not true.
stewart_read: Customer discloses a prior pitch (possibly a different company or a Dominion-branded program) that misrepresented terms. The rep briefly reacts but never probes who made this claim or what company/program it was, losing competitive intelligence.
coaching_implication: Coach a 10-second probe: 'who told you that, and was that Ion or another company?' — this is free competitive intel the closer would want.

quote: And and the program broke for twenty five years. That's $30,000. No way I'm paying that.
stewart_read: This is the clearest 'I can't afford it' framing in the call and it goes completely unanswered before the customer ends the call — the rep has no response logged between this line and the customer's exit request.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have recognized the call was already lost and chosen not to push further, which could be a reasonable de-escalation strategic choice given the customer's repeated firm refusals.
coaching_implication: Even in a likely-lost call, a brief acknowledgment-plus-reframe attempt costs nothing; silence here reads as giving up rather than closing gracefully.

quote: But I'm just gonna say, you could just cross me off, please.
stewart_read: The call ends with an opt-out request and the rep simply complies without any attempt at a protocol-appropriate small-ask or clarification of what specifically turned the customer off, closing the door on any future re-engagement.
alternative_hypothesis: Given the customer's firmness and repeated explicit refusals, continuing to push could plausibly damage the brand relationship further, so compliance may be the correct de-escalation call.
coaching_implication: Discuss with rep whether a brief, respectful acknowledgment of the specific concern (e.g., 'I hear you on the $30k number — I'll note that and take you off') would leave a better final impression without extending the call.
